title: OpenAI Chief Scientist Proposes Drawing a Line for Industry-Wide Model Development: Where Capability Growth Should Stop Depends First on Whether Humans Can Keep It in Check

content_html:
The front-runner is the first to shout, “Everyone, slow down a little.” That scene is now playing out at the front lines of the AI industry. OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki published a piece proposing that AI companies should agree to place limits on increasingly powerful models until researchers have better ways to understand and monitor their behavior. His vision is an industry-wide standard: companies would jointly commit not to cross a drawn capability line before meeting specific safety requirements.

How is that line supposed to be drawn? Pachocki offers a concrete lever: perplexity. This technical metric measures a model’s ability to predict the next segment of text; the lower the number, the deeper the model’s grasp of language patterns. He proposes that companies set common limits based on metrics such as perplexity, with developers pledging not to break through those limits until “the ability to understand and monitor AI behavior reaches a specific milestone.” In plain terms, it ties “how powerful the model is” to “whether humans can keep an eye on it”: the former’s eligibility to keep rising depends on whether the latter can keep up. However, he did not say what level the initial limits should be set at or when implementation should begin. The blueprint is still missing two key coordinates.

He is pushing this urgently because of a very tight timeline. Pachocki warns that as early as 2027, AI could begin to accelerate its own evolution, and that this pace could outstrip the speed at which researchers improve their ability to monitor and understand it—once the race becomes like that, the reins in humanity’s hands are quietly loosening.

The proposal has been endorsed by the person at the helm. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman publicly expressed support, calling the piece “the most important thing OpenAI has published in some time,” and argued that agreeing on common limits will help ensure “safety and control.” On the same day, Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman also reposted the article, announcing that Microsoft fully supports this transparency initiative. The fact that two top industry companies have spoken up in succession is certainly a good start, but for the limits to truly take hold, it will ultimately depend on whether other players are willing to let the same red line govern the accelerator.
